chapters.title: Chapter 3: Behavioral Economics in Pricing, Business, and Negotiation

lessons.title: Anchoring in Pricing: Why MRP and Flat 70% Off Work on Everyone

children.text: A kurta hangs on a rack with a tag reading "MRP ₹2,499" struck through, "Now ₹749" printed below it in red. You do the mental maths: 70% off, a genuine steal. You almost never ask the one question that actually matters: has this kurta ever sold for ₹2,499 to anyone, ever? For most shoppers, the answer doesn't matter, because the ₹2,499 has already done its job the instant your eyes landed on it. This lesson is about anchoring, the third heuristic named in Kahneman and Tversky's original 1974 paper, held back from Chapter 1 specifically so you could see it where it does the most damage: on a price tag.

body.text: The first number you see, even one you know is arbitrary or manipulated, pulls every judgment you make afterward toward itself. People do adjust away from an anchor once they notice it, but almost never enough. A wildly inflated MRP doesn't need to be believed to work. It only needs to be seen first.

markDefs.definition: The tendency for an initial number, even an arbitrary or irrelevant one, to heavily influence a later estimate or decision, because people adjust away from that first number but consistently not far enough.

children.text: with an experiment involving a wheel of fortune rigged to stop on either 10 or 65. Participants spun the wheel, noted the number it landed on, and were then asked an entirely unrelated question: what percentage of countries in the United Nations were African nations? Participants who had just seen the wheel land on 10 gave a median estimate around 25%. Participants who saw it land on 65 gave a median estimate around 45%. A random number from a rigged wheel, which participants knew was random, still pulled their answers toward itself by a wide margin. If a meaningless number moves a factual estimate this much, imagine what a carefully chosen, deliberately inflated price tag can do to a purchase decision.
MRP: India's Most Successful Permanent Anchor

markDefs.definition: The Maximum Retail Price, the highest price at which a pre-packaged product can legally be sold in India, printed on every package under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. It sets a ceiling, not a typical or fair selling price.

children.text: Under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, every pre-packaged product sold in India must print an

. The law was written for consumer protection: to guarantee nobody is ever charged more than a fixed ceiling. Nothing in the law says MRP has to bear any relationship to what a product typically sells for, and in categories like branded apparel, that gap is routinely enormous. A retailer can set MRP wherever they like, then "discount" from it by whatever percentage makes the deal look most dramatic, while the actual rupee amount a shopper pays barely moves from one "sale" to the next. The MRP isn't describing the product's value. It is manufacturing your anchor.
Flat X% Off: Same Anchor, a More Dramatic Wrapper

"Flat 70% Off" is more persuasive than simply stating the final price, because a percentage forces you to run the anchoring calculation yourself, in your own head, using the retailer's own inflated starting number. You do the work of feeling impressed. Here is exactly how loosely that dramatic percentage can sit on top of a completely ordinary profit margin.

body.caption: If this kurta actually costs the retailer ₹350 to produce and distribute, their profit is ₹600 − ₹350 = ₹250, a margin of ₹250 ÷ ₹350 ≈ 71% over cost, comfortably healthy, despite a headline discount that sounds close to giving the product away.

body.title: Check a second "steep discount"
body.prompt: A pair of jeans costs a retailer ₹450 to produce and distribute. The tag reads "MRP ₹3,000, Flat 80% Off, Pay ₹600." What is the retailer's profit margin on that ₹600 sale, as a percentage of their ₹450 cost?
body.explanation: Profit = ₹600 − ₹450 = ₹150. Margin over cost = ₹150 ÷ ₹450 ≈ 33.3%. An "80% off" tag and a healthy, perfectly ordinary retail margin are not contradictions. MRP and cost price were never connected to begin with.

body.text: Notice what the discount percentage never tells you: the retailer's cost, a fair market price for a comparable unbranded item, or what this exact product sold for last month. A discount percentage only ever compares a price to itself. Comparing it to anything else is work the anchor is specifically designed to make you skip.

children.text: Anchoring Beyond Retail: Salary Negotiation and Real Estate

Anchoring is not a retail-only trick. Negotiation researchers have repeatedly found that whoever states the first number in a salary or price negotiation pulls the final settlement toward their own figure, which is exactly why experienced negotiators are trained to make the first offer rather than wait to react to someone else's. A classic study by Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale found that real-estate agents touring an identical property, given identical information packets except for the listing price shown, gave significantly different valuations depending on that listing price, even though the agents insisted, confidently, that the listing price had not influenced their expert judgment at all. Lesson 3 of this chapter goes deep on how to use, and resist, anchoring specifically in negotiation. For now, the point is simpler: the very first number on the table, in a shop or across a negotiating table, is rarely neutral information.

children.text: Defending Against Anchors: The Adjustment You're Not Making Enough Of

Knowing about anchoring does not automatically protect you from it. The fix is procedural, not willpower. Build your own reference price before you see the seller's: check a comparable unbranded product, search the same item on a different platform, or simply ask what you would pay for this if there were no tag on it at all. Treat any percentage-off figure as meaningless on its own, and convert it to the actual rupee amount before deciding whether that amount is worth it. In a negotiation, make the first offer yourself whenever you reasonably can, so you are setting the anchor rather than adjusting insufficiently from someone else's.

body.title: Is this really a deal?
body.scenario: An online furniture site lists a study table: "MRP ₹18,999, Deal Price ₹5,999, You Save 68%." A quick search shows near-identical tables from smaller, unbranded sellers on the same site consistently priced between ₹5,200 and ₹6,500, with no strikethrough MRP shown at all.
body.prompt: Using what this lesson covered, how should a buyer actually evaluate this listing?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The ₹18,999 MRP and the "68% off" figure are anchoring devices. Neither number tells the buyer anything about what the table is actually worth.
2. The genuinely useful data point is the comparison the buyer already found: near-identical unbranded tables selling in the same ₹5,200 to ₹6,500 range, with no inflated MRP theatre attached at all.
3. Against that real comparison, ₹5,999 looks like an unremarkable, roughly market-rate price, not a 68% windfall. The size of the discount percentage carries no information once an independent reference point exists.
4. The correct decision process is to evaluate ₹5,999 on its own merits against comparable options, exactly as the buyer already did, and to treat the MRP and "you save" framing as marketing copy rather than as evidence.

body.title: Anchoring, or something else?
body.question: A shopper sees a food delivery app default to the most expensive delivery speed option, pre-selected, with slower and cheaper options listed below it in smaller text. After noticing the expensive option is pre-selected, the shopper switches to a cheaper one in two seconds. Which mechanism was primarily at work in the pre-selection itself, before the shopper switched?
options: Anchoring, because the pre-selected option quietly set the reference point for what a normal delivery fee looks like
The default effect, because the pre-selected option is what happens if the shopper does nothing at all
The endowment effect, because the shopper already feels they own the selected option
Present bias, because the shopper wants their food to arrive quickly
body.explanation: A pre-selected option that requires zero action to keep is a textbook default from Lesson 1 of Chapter 2, not anchoring. Anchoring would instead be at work if, say, the app displayed the most expensive plan's price first and boldest, shaping how reasonable the other prices feel by comparison, even if none of them were pre-selected.

body.title: Name the heuristic
body.textWithBlank: The tendency for an initial number, even an arbitrary one, to heavily influence a later judgment because people adjust away from it but not far enough, is called ___ and adjustment.
body.explanation: Anchoring and adjustment was one of the three original heuristics named in Kahneman and Tversky's 1974 paper, alongside representativeness and availability, both covered in Chapter 1.

children.text: Kahneman and Tversky chose a rigged wheel of fortune precisely because it removed every possible objection that the anchor carried real information. A price tag could plausibly reflect cost. A real estate listing could plausibly reflect the seller's honest assessment. A number generated by a wheel participants watched spin at random carries no information whatsoever, and knowing this did not stop it from moving people's answers. That is what made the result so hard for classical economic theory to explain away: if a meaningless number can anchor a judgment this strongly, a carefully chosen, seemingly meaningful one like an MRP is likely to work even better.

body.label: How far a random wheel spin shifted estimates
body.context: Median guesses for the share of African UN member countries, after participants saw a rigged wheel land on 10 versus 65, in Kahneman and Tversky's original experiment.

cards.definition: The tendency for an initial number to heavily pull a later judgment toward itself, because people adjust away from it but not enough.
The legal ceiling price printed on pre-packaged Indian products under the Legal Metrology Rules, 2011. It sets a maximum, not a typical or fair selling price.
A framing device that compares a price only to itself (its own MRP), carrying no information about cost, fair value, or comparable alternatives.
The finding that whoever states the first number in a negotiation tends to pull the final settlement closer to that number.
A price or value estimate built before seeing a seller's anchor, from comparable products or alternative sources, used to defend against anchoring.

points: Anchoring means an initial number, even one known to be arbitrary, heavily shapes every judgment that follows, because people adjust away from it but consistently not enough.

India's MRP system is a near-permanent, legally mandated anchor: a ceiling price with no required connection to cost or typical selling price, which retailers can set high specifically to make any discount look dramatic.
A steep discount percentage and a comfortable profit margin can, and routinely do, coexist, because MRP and actual production cost were never linked in the first place.
The same mechanism drives negotiation outcomes and real-estate valuations, which is why experienced negotiators try to make the first offer rather than react to someone else's.

The only reliable defence is procedural: build an independent reference price before seeing the seller's number, and convert every percentage-off claim into an actual rupee amount before judging whether it's worth it.
